summary: Reserves the Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) from EAP for the sole purpose of deriving root keys. Root keys are master keys that can be used for several purposes identified by usage definitions. The memo also specifies a way to avoid conflicts between root keys by deriving them in a way tied to their intended use.

eli5.summary: One master key can be used to make many separate keys, each only for one job, like a master recipe that yields different dishes without mixing them up.

questions: what is the emsk in eap
subtitle: How the spare key from EAP is turned into separate root keys, one per purpose, without the purposes interfering.

tldr.problem: EAP produces an Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) but left it reserved for unspecified future uses. If several uses each derived keys from it in their own way, a weakness in one could affect the others.
tldr.mechanism: The EMSK is reserved solely for deriving root keys. Each usage gets its own root key through a key derivation function fed with a unique key label, so that the derived keys are cryptographically separate.
tldr.outcome: New uses of EAP key material can be defined independently. The RFC also defines Domain-Specific Root Keys for keys limited to one key management domain.

today: RFC 5295 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it. Its header notes that it updates RFC 5247.

sections.title: The Problem and the Terms
sections.content:
EAP defines two kinds of keying material, the Master Session Key (MSK) and the Extended Master Session Key (EMSK). The EAP specification assumes the MSK serves a single purpose at a single device, and it reserves the EMSK for future use. This RFC fixes that use: the EMSK is to be used solely for deriving root keys.

A usage definition is a specific application of the key material, such as hand-off between access points or mobile IP authentication. A Usage-Specific Root Key (USRK) is keying material derived from the EMSK for one usage definition. A Domain-Specific Root Key (DSRK) is derived from the EMSK and restricted to a key management domain, the set of systems authorized to use key material derived from that key.

The RFC does not define how USRKs are used. It defines a framework so that different usages can be developed independently, with the security of one having minimal or no effect on another.
sections.eli5: A special master key is saved only for making other keys. Each job gets its own key made from it, and the master key itself is never handed out.

sections.title: Where These Keys Fit
sections.content:
Keys from the EMSK are expected to be used in protocols tied to network access, such as handover optimizations, whose scope is usually the endpoints of the lower layers carrying EAP packets. Relying on them for higher-layer application security is inappropriate. Applications should not assume which lower-layer technology serves a hop, and application endpoints may differ from EAP endpoints.

The RFC therefore says it is NOT RECOMMENDED to use keys derived from the EMSK as an exclusive security mechanism unless their usage is inherently and permanently tied to the lower layer where network access authentication happened.

Keys derived from EAP are pair-wise by nature. They are not directly suitable for multicast or other group uses, although they can be used in protocols that distribute group keys. Defining such protocols is out of scope.
sections.eli5: These keys are meant for the door you walked through to get onto the network, not for locking up everything you do once you are inside.

sections.title: Cryptographic Separation
sections.content:
Derived keys must be cryptographically separate: given any derived key, it is computationally infeasible to derive any other, or to derive the EMSK. Without this, a usage's security would depend on every other usage drawing from the same EMSK.

Two obvious methods are a key stream from a pseudo-random function (PRF), or giving the PRF a different input for each key. The RFC prefers the second because child keys can then be derived in any order, independently. That requires the extra input to be coordinated so that no two usages derive the same key.

The RFC requires that:

  • It MUST be infeasible to compute the EMSK from any root key.
  • Any root key MUST be cryptographically separate from any other root key derived from the same EMSK or DSRK.
  • USRK and DSRK derivations MUST be coordinated so two usages or two domains never derive the same key.
  • No domain can obtain a USRK by providing a domain name identical to a Usage Key Label.
sections.eli5: If someone steals one key from the set, they should learn nothing about the others or about the master. Each key is made with a different secret ingredient so they cannot be swapped.

sections.title: The Derivation Function
sections.content:
A USRK comes from the EMSK, a key label, optional data and an output length. The key label is a printable ASCII string unique to each usage definition, at most 255 octets and normally of the form label-string@specorg. A NULL octet follows the label so that one label being a prefix of another (such as "foobar" and "foobarExtendedV2") cannot cause a collision.

The KDF MUST handle at least 2048 octets of optional data, accept input keys of up to 256 bytes, and produce at least 2048 octets of output. USRKs MUST be at least 64 octets long. The same KDF MUST be used for all derivations from a given EMSK.

The default KDF is the PRF+ expansion from RFC 4306 using HMAC-SHA-256. Because PRF+ is defined for 255 iterations, it can produce up to 8160 octets. An authenticated key exchange, such as an EAP method, MAY name a favored KDF that overrides the default.

The EMSK also gets a name, derived from the EAP Session-ID. Keys derived from the EMSK are by default referred to by that EMSKname and the context of their usage. USRKs MAY be named explicitly.
sections.eli5: The recipe takes the master key, a unique name tag for the job, and some extras, and stirs them. A different tag gives a totally different key, and the same tag always gives the same one.

sections.title: Domain-Specific Root Keys
sections.content:
A DSRK is a USRK with the key label dsrk@ietf.org and optional data holding an ASCII string naming the key management domain. It MUST be at least 64 octets long. From a DSRK, usages derive Domain-Specific Usage-Specific Root Keys (DSUSRKs) with the same kind of KDF, so a domain can derive keys for its own usages without ever holding the EMSK.

Usages that use a DSRK must define how the peer learns the domain label. A multi-domain usage must define how DSRKs and DSUSRKs reach the different domains. To let EMSKname refer to keys derived from a DSRK, the EMSKname SHOULD be sent along with the DSRK.

If only one domain should perform a function, the usage SHOULD NOT be multi-domain. Where only some domains are authorized, the others should not receive the DSRK, only the DSUSRKs for usages they are authorized for.
sections.eli5: A domain gets its own sub-master key. It can make keys for its own jobs, but it never sees the real master and cannot make keys for other domains.

sections.title: Rules for Usages and EAP Systems
sections.content:
A usage definition must say whether it is domain-enabled, MUST define distinct key labels and optional data, MUST define the length of its root keys, and MUST define how it uses them. It MUST NOT use the EMSK directly or in any way other than deriving root keys, and SHOULD NOT require caching of the EMSK. Root keys are RECOMMENDED to be at least 64 octets, as long as the EMSK.

Root key lifetimes should not exceed that of the EMSK. When a new EMSK arrives from a later EAP exchange, usages should switch to the new root keys as soon as possible. The EMSK never leaves the EAP peer and server. When root keys are delivered to another entity, the EMSKname and the lifetime MUST also be transported.

The EAP system must keep the EMSK secret, keep it in a protected location, make it unique for each EAP session, and have the EAP method provide an identifier for the transaction. New usage definitions MUST NOT use the MSK, and implementations MUST prevent combinations where more than one usage uses the MSK.
sections.eli5: Anyone who wants a key must register their own name tag, say how long their key is and how it will be used. Nobody may touch the master key directly.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The strength of derived keys never exceeds the strength of the EMSK. The KDF is meant to keep USRKs separate, so compromising one does not compromise other USRKs or the EMSK, and the RFC says it is believed the KDF chosen provides this. Few root keys are expected, and no randomness is added in deriving them beyond the labels. So if many keys will be derived from a root key, each root-to-child derivation should add fresh random numbers.

Secret keys that are distributed MUST have integrity and confidentiality protected and go only to authenticated, authorized parties. The RFC defines no key transport mechanism, which is left to usage definitions.

IANA gets two new registries. USRK Key Labels are printable US-ASCII, at most 64 characters, assigned by Specification Required, with experimental1, experimental2, private1 and private2 reserved and EMSK and dsrk@ietf.org reserved by this document. EMSK PRF numbers run 0 to 255, where 1 is HMAC-SHA-256 PRF+ (default).
sections.eli5: The derived keys can never be stronger than the master. The rules about labels are like a signup sheet so no two jobs ever pick the same name tag.

data.title: Root key derivation
data.code:
USRK = KDF(EMSK, key label | "\0" | optional data | length)

  | denotes concatenation
  "\0" is a NULL octet (0x00 in hex)
  length is a 2-octet unsigned integer in network byte order
